title: How do you guys turn a strategy in your head into something testable?
author: Few-Negotiation-3974
selftext:
I keep running into this problem where a setup looks simple when I'm watching the chart but gets complicated when I try to describe the exact rules.  
  
I know a “good” entry when I see one, but telling why it’s a “good” entry is something else again.  
  
For those of you who’ve automated your trading, how did you get around this? Did you start with really basic rules and build from there or try to replicate exactly how you trade manually?

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body:
I’d start by saving examples of both trades you’d take and trades that almost qualify. The near-misses are usually more useful because they force you to explain what actually made the setup valid, using only what you knew at the time.

Turn that into the simplest rules you can and test the ugly first version. Add conditions one at a time, and only keep them if they help on unseen data after fees and slippage.

If a rule only makes sense after the move, it’s hindsight, not a strategy.

replies.author: Few-Negotiation-3974
replies.body: I didn't think to include trades that are briefly dropped, which might actually make the rules clearer.

replies.author: Fynca
replies.body: Exactly. Those almost-trades are usually where the rule gets clearest. If you can name the one condition that made you pass in real time, you’ve probably found a real filter instead of a story added after the fact.

comments.author: zurichbtc
comments.body: I like to reverse engineer it and start a conversation with my pref LLM with "I have a vague idea in mind but need your help in articulating it"

comments.author: Rare_Inflation3178
comments.body:
I’d start with the dumbest version of the idea you can actually define. Entry conditions, invalidation, exit. Test that first and only add complexity if it improves out-of-sample.  
LLMs are actually pretty useful here. I use them to turn “this setup looks good” into explicit features and rules I can test.  
I ended up building a whole workflow around that problem because translating intuition into something falsifiable was harder than coming up with the idea in the first place.
